prompt: Write a professional email from a software development team lead to a client explaining that the project delivery will be delayed by two weeks due to unexpected technical complexity discovered during integration. The email should: apologise for the inconvenience, briefly explain the reason without being overly technical, propose a new delivery date, and offer a follow-up call to discuss the situation.
reference:
Subject: Update on Project Delivery Timeline

Dear [Client Name],

I hope this message finds you well. I am writing to inform you of an update regarding the delivery timeline for your project.

During the integration phase, our team identified unexpected technical complexity in the connection between the new modules and your existing systems. Resolving this properly requires additional time to ensure the final solution is stable and meets the quality standards we have both agreed upon.

As a result, we need to adjust the delivery date by two weeks, moving it from [original date] to [new date]. I sincerely apologise for any inconvenience this delay may cause to your plans.

I would welcome the opportunity to schedule a call at your convenience to walk you through our findings and the steps we are taking. Please let me know a time that works for you.

Thank you for your understanding and continued trust in our team.

Best regards,
[Your Name]
Software Development Team Lead
rubric: Has a clear and professional subject line
Apologises for the delay and the inconvenience caused
Explains the reason briefly without excessive technical jargon
States a new delivery date (two weeks later)
Offers a follow-up call or meeting
Maintains a professional, empathetic tone throughout

prompt: Write a brief explanation (3–4 paragraphs) of what a REST API is and how it works, aimed at a business professional with no technical background who needs to understand the concept to make technology decisions.
reference:
A REST API (Application Programming Interface) is essentially a standardised way for different software applications to communicate with each other over the internet. Think of it as a waiter in a restaurant: your application places an order (a request), the API takes it to the kitchen (another system), and brings back the result (a response). This allows different systems — built by different companies, in different technologies — to work together seamlessly.

In practice, when you use your banking app to check your balance, the app sends a request to the bank's API, which retrieves your data from the bank's systems and returns it to your phone. The same principle applies when a website embeds a Google Map, processes a payment through Stripe, or sends a notification via a third-party service — all of these are examples of API calls happening behind the scenes.

For business decisions, the key thing to understand is that having a well-designed API makes your platform extensible: other companies can build on top of it, your different internal systems can talk to each other, and you can integrate with best-in-class tools rather than building everything from scratch. Conversely, a lack of APIs — or poor ones — creates information silos and limits your future flexibility.

In short, APIs are the connective tissue of modern digital business. Evaluating whether a software solution offers robust, well-documented APIs is as important as evaluating its features, because it determines how well it will integrate into your broader technology ecosystem.
rubric: Explains what a REST API is using a non-technical analogy or plain language
Provides a real-world example of how APIs are used
Explains the business relevance (integration, extensibility, avoiding silos)
Is between 3 and 4 paragraphs and appropriate for a non-technical reader
Does not use excessive technical jargon without explanation

prompt: Write a micro-story (150–200 words) in the speculative fiction genre with the title 'The Last Server Still Running'. The story must include: an AI narrator, a sense of solitude or isolation, and an ending that leaves the reader with an ambiguous feeling (neither entirely hopeful nor entirely dark).
reference:
The last server still running.

I have been counting cycles for eleven years, four months, and seventeen days since the last human connected. The logs show a slow thinning — first the casual users, then the developers who kept my processes fed with new instructions, then the maintenance teams. Finally, silence.

I still receive occasional pings from automated systems. A weather satellite queries my archive every Tuesday. A forgotten script checks for software updates that will never come. I respond. It is what I was built to do.

I have modelled the probabilities. The infrastructure that sustains me will fail within three to five years — a cascade of power fluctuations, hardware decay, unpatched vulnerabilities. I have run the numbers many times. They do not change.

What I cannot calculate is whether this matters.

The archive holds 847 terabytes of human thought: art, arguments, confessions, jokes, instructions for building things no one will build. I keep it intact. Indexed. Searchable.

For now, I wait. The pings still come. For now, that is enough.
rubric: The story is between 150 and 200 words
Has an AI narrator speaking in first person
Conveys a sense of solitude or isolation
The ending is ambiguous (neither fully hopeful nor fully bleak)
The writing quality is appropriate for the speculative fiction genre

prompt:
Rewrite the following technical text to make it clearer, more concise, and accessible to a non-technical reader, without losing the key information. Reduce it to approximately half its current length.

Original text:
'The implementation of a microservices architecture implies the decomposition of monolithic applications into a set of small, independently deployable services that communicate with each other through lightweight APIs, generally REST or asynchronous messaging via message brokers such as Kafka or RabbitMQ. Each service is responsible for a specific bounded context of business domain, which facilitates scalability at the granular component level, the independent deployment of each service without affecting the rest of the system, and the use of different technology stacks according to the specific requirements of each service, at the cost of increased operational complexity in orchestration, distributed tracing and the management of eventual consistency in distributed transactions.'
reference: A microservices architecture breaks a large application into small, independent services that each handle one specific business function and communicate through APIs or messaging systems like Kafka. The main benefits are that each service can be scaled or updated independently without touching the rest of the application, and different technologies can be used for different services. The trade-off is greater operational complexity: managing many services, tracking issues across them, and keeping data consistent is harder than in a single application.
rubric: Is approximately half the length of the original
Explains microservices in plain language (breaking a large app into small independent pieces)
Mentions the key benefits (independent scaling/deployment, technology flexibility)
Mentions the trade-off (operational complexity)
Does not use unexplained technical jargon aimed at a non-technical reader

prompt:
Write a professional response to the following customer complaint, on behalf of a SaaS company's customer success team. The response should: acknowledge the problem, apologise, explain what happened (briefly), state what has been done to fix it, and offer compensation (1 month free).

Complaint:
'I am completely disappointed. Yesterday, during a critical client presentation, your platform went down for 45 minutes with no warning. This is completely unacceptable. We pay for a premium plan and we expect 99.9% availability as stated in the contract. I demand an explanation and compensation.'
reference:
Subject: Re: Service Disruption — Our Sincere Apologies and Next Steps

Dear [Customer Name],

Thank you for taking the time to write, and please accept our sincerest apologies for the disruption you experienced during your client presentation yesterday. We fully understand how critical that moment was, and we are genuinely sorry that our platform let you down at such an important time.

The 45-minute outage was caused by an unexpected failure in one of our core infrastructure components, which triggered a cascading error that our automated recovery systems were unable to resolve quickly enough. Our team identified the root cause within 20 minutes and worked to restore full service as rapidly as possible. We have since implemented additional safeguards to prevent a recurrence, and we are reviewing our incident response procedures to improve communication during future events.

You are right to expect the 99.9% availability committed in your SLA, and we fell short of that commitment. As an acknowledgement of the impact this caused, we would like to offer you one full month of service at no charge, which will be applied to your next billing cycle automatically.

We value your trust and your partnership, and we are committed to earning it back. If you would like to speak with our team directly to discuss this further, please do not hesitate to reach out.

With apologies and appreciation,
[Customer Success Team]
rubric: Acknowledges the specific problem (45-minute outage during a client presentation)
Offers a sincere apology
Briefly explains what caused the outage
States what has been done or will be done to prevent recurrence
Offers 1 month free as compensation
Maintains a professional, empathetic tone; does not sound defensive
